title: Does Alpha School Work for Regular Kids?
author: Dan Meyer
summary: Math educator Dan Meyer investigates whether Alpha School's widely publicized claim -- that its AI-driven "2 Hour Learning" model produces students who "grow 2.6 times faster" than peers -- survives being separated from its highly selective admissions process. Alpha School charges $40,000-$75,000 in tuition and screens for students who are self-motivated, "coachable," neurotypical, able-bodied, and free of disciplinary history, making it impossible to know from its results alone whether the model or the selection is doing the work. Meyer finds a natural test case in Unbound Academy, an Arizona public charter school founded by Alpha's own leadership that imports the 2 Hour Learning model but, as a public charter, cannot legally replicate Alpha's selective admissions and is free to any resident. Drawing on Unbound's own charter-application targets and its publicly posted board materials, Meyer shows the school's first-year results badly missed its own projections and underperformed Arizona state averages in both math and ELA, concluding that the "quasi-experiment" Alpha's founders set up themselves suggests it is far harder to produce successful students than to select them in advance.
points: Alpha School's headline claim -- that its AI-driven "2 Hour Learning" model helps students "grow 2.6 times faster" than peers -- cannot be separated from an admissions process that screens for self-motivated, "coachable," typically-developing students whose parents can pay $40,000 to $75,000 in tuition.

Unbound Academy, an Arizona public charter founded by Alpha's own leadership to import the 2 Hour Learning model without Alpha's selective admissions, functions as an unplanned natural experiment isolating the model from the selection effect.

Unbound Academy's own charter application projected 60% math proficiency (from a 34% baseline) and 65% ELA proficiency (from a 40% baseline) within its first two to three years; it instead posted 10% math and 28% ELA proficiency in year one, below even the Arizona state averages.
Meyer's conclusion is that Alpha's own quasi-experiment argues against its central marketing claim: it is far harder to make successful students than it is to select them in advance.
quotes: Media coverage of Alpha School has generally focused on its claim that it educates children much faster than traditional models, specifically that it helps students "grow 2.6 times faster than peers on nationally normed MAP tests" and do it in two hours instead of six.
I'll meet the kid, and I'm like, listen, kiddo, this is up to you," says admissions director Cara Wilkinson. "This is not about your parents. This is about you.

Unbound Academy's enrollment application is, by law, much less selective than Alpha School's. A parent doesn't have to attest that their student is neurotypical, able-bodied, and well-behaved. They only have to meet the much lower bar of geographic residency.

Unbound Academy projected 60% proficiency in math off a baseline of 34% and ended the year with 10% compared to an Arizona state average of 34%. They projected 65% proficiency in ELA off a baseline of 40% and ended with 28% compared to an Arizona state average of 42%.

But Alpha School has not become nationally famous for its claims to grow student learning in some bounded capacity. It has become famous for the claims of its founder and principal that student learning is "limitless," and, indeed, that the Alpha School model will take students to the outer edges of academic achievement.
Their outcomes indicate that it is far harder to make successful students than it is to select them in advance.
